opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the central challenge is that we've moved from a world of narrow, well-specified tasks to models that are general-purpose, and our evaluation methodology hasn't really caught up. In classical machine learning, you had a clear prediction problem, a held-out test set drawn from the same distribution as your training data, and a well-defined loss function. You could make fairly rigorous statements about generalization. With large language models, almost none of that holds cleanly.

First, there's the question of what the task even is. These models are used for summarization, coding, question answering, creative writing, giving advice, and the space of possible uses is essentially open-ended. So any benchmark is a tiny slice of a vast space of behaviors, and it's not obvious how performance on that slice generalizes to the ways people actually use the model.

Second, there's contamination. These models are trained on enormous swaths of the internet, and benchmarks tend to end up on the internet. So it becomes very hard to know whether a model is reasoning its way to an answer or has effectively seen the test before. The basic separation between training and test data that the field relied on for decades has gotten very blurry.

Third, many of the properties we care most about, like fairness, privacy, robustness, and truthfulness, are notoriously hard to define, let alone measure. Even in simpler settings, fairness has many competing definitions that are mathematically incompatible. In a generative setting, where the output is free-form text rather than a yes-or-no decision, it's even harder to say precisely what a fair or unbiased response is. You often end up relying on human judgment or on another model acting as the judge, and both of those bring their own noise and biases.

And finally, there's a kind of Goodhart's law dynamic. Once a benchmark becomes a target, people optimize toward it, sometimes inadvertently, and the benchmark stops measuring what it was designed to measure. So I'd say the challenge is less about building any single good metric and more about building an evaluation science, with principled ways of defining the properties we care about, sampling the space of uses sensibly, and being honest about what a given number does and doesn't tell us.

r001.rationale: The response says LLM uses are essentially open-ended and benchmarks cover only a tiny slice of the vast range of behaviors.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the central challenge is that with large language models, we've largely lost the thing that made benchmarks meaningful in the first place, which is a well-defined task with a well-defined notion of ground truth.

For most of the history of machine learning, a benchmark was something like ImageNet or a spam classification dataset. There was a clear input, a clear label, and we could all agree on what it meant to get it right. You held out a test set, you measured accuracy, and the number actually told you something about generalization. Language models are generative and open-ended. If you ask one to summarize a document or write an argument, there isn't a single correct output, and reasonable people will disagree about what counts as good. So the first problem is that the thing we're trying to measure is often not crisply defined.

The second problem, which is related, is contamination. These models are trained on an enormous fraction of the public internet, and the benchmarks themselves are on the public internet. So the clean separation between training and test, which is the entire scientific basis for a held-out evaluation, has essentially collapsed. When a model scores well on a benchmark, you often can't tell whether it generalized or whether it saw the answers.

And then there's a third issue that I think about a lot coming from the theory side, which is that benchmarks become targets. The moment a number matters, people optimize for it, and the benchmark stops measuring what it was designed to measure. That's Goodhart's law, but it's especially acute here because the models are so capable and the labs are so motivated.

So where I'd like to see the field go is toward evaluations that are more like statistical tests than leaderboards. Things with explicit hypotheses, fresh or adversarially generated instances, and some honest accounting of uncertainty. And in the areas I care most about, fairness, privacy, and safety, I think we need to stop asking whether a model is "good" in some aggregate sense and ask much more specific, auditable questions about how it behaves on particular populations and particular kinds of inputs. Those are the questions that actually matter when these systems are deployed.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs are generative and open-ended, but uses that to explain why outputs lack a single correct answer. It does not identify the open-ended range of possible inputs as a benchmarking difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is figuring out what we actually want to measure. With a narrowly defined prediction problem, you can often agree on what constitutes an error and then measure how frequently it occurs. With a large language model, the range of tasks is so broad that even defining success becomes difficult. A response might be factually correct but unhelpful, or helpful in one context and inappropriate in another.

And that gets especially difficult when we care about properties like fairness or safety. Those aren't single quantities with universally agreed-upon definitions. You have to specify the context, whose interests you're considering, and what tradeoffs you're willing to accept. Choosing a metric doesn't make those choices disappear.

So I would be skeptical of any single number that purports to tell us how good a language model is. We need evaluations tied to particular uses, with a clear account of what they measure and what they leave out. The challenge is making sure that progress on the benchmark actually corresponds to progress on the thing we care about.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs cover a broad range of tasks, but it does not identify the open-ended range of possible inputs as a source of difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is that we’re trying to evaluate systems whose range of possible uses is enormously broad, and we often haven’t specified precisely what good behavior means. For a particular classification task, you can define a distribution, collect labeled examples, and measure error. With a language model, a response might be factually correct but unhelpful, or helpful in one context and inappropriate in another. It’s hard to collapse all of that into a single number.

And then there’s the gap between performance on a benchmark and performance in deployment. If everyone is optimizing against the same tests, improvements on those tests don’t necessarily tell you how the model will behave on genuinely new problems. So I think we need more targeted evaluations, tied to particular uses and populations, and a clearer understanding of what each metric actually establishes. A benchmark can give you useful evidence, but it isn’t a general certificate of reliability.

r001.rationale: The response says LLMs have an enormously broad range of possible uses and discusses genuinely new problems, but it does not identify the open-ended range of possible inputs as a source of benchmark difficulty.
